entries.title: White Sox’ competitive turnaround slows down prospect parade
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — Any other year of this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> rebuild, shortstop prospect Jacob Gonzalez would already be with the big-league squad by this point of the season.</p><p>The Sox’ 2023 first-rounder is slashing a torrid .299/.409/.603 at Triple-A Charlotte with 15 home runs, nine doubles and seven stolen bases.</p><p>The only problem for Gonzalez is the Sox have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/18/munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-miguel-vargas-white-sox-home-runs" target="_blank" ><u>one of the most productive infields</u></a> in baseball at the moment among Colson Montgomery, Miguel Vargas, Chase Meidroth and Munetaka Murakami.</p><p>“Jacob is playing as good as he can play,” Sox farm director Paul Janish said. “There’s a lot of options right now, so he’s doing everything he can and definitely has himself in the conversation.”</p><p>It’s a roster crunch the Sox are getting more familiar with after a few years of living with glaring MLB roster holes, meaning a little bit longer of a wait for some of their most anticipated talent.</p><p>“It’s a really good problem to have,” Janish said. “Generally speaking, the players figure that out. They will show us who’s supposed to be the shortstop. But having a bunch of options is a really good thing especially the way major league rosters operate these days.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">There he goes again!! Jacob Gonzalez 💣 <a href="https://t.co/NL5YTBiWEy">pic.twitter.com/NL5YTBiWEy</a></p>— Charlotte Knights (@KnightsBaseball) <a href="https://twitter.com/KnightsBaseball/status/2056869986547769805?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>There’s a clearer path to Rate Field in the outfield, as second baseman-turned-left fielder <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/23/sam-antonacci-white-sox-hit-by-pitch-leadoff" target="_blank" ><u>Sam Antonacci</u></a> can attest. There would probably be more movement there if Tristan Peters weren’t manning center as adequately as he has (.256/.316/.368).</p><p>Top prospect Braden Montgomery figures to get his shot in the Sox’ outfield at some point this summer. He’s hit .243/.321/.400 with two homers in his first 18 Triple-A games.</p><p>“Braden answered every challenge we’ve given him at this point,” Janish said. “I know a lot of people will look at the offensive numbers, which are good, but he’s played as good of defense as we’ve seen from him in the year and half we’ve had him in the organization.”</p><p>The same goes for Rikuu Nishida (.347/.454/.395), a second baseman who’s taking reps across the outfield for the Knights.</p><p>“He’s one of the best baseball players that we have in our organization,” Janish said of Nishida, a native of Osaka, Japan. “He is contagious in the best way.”</p><p>While the Sox have had a rotating bullpen cast between Charlotte and Chicago, some movement could come to the rotation, too, if Erick Fedde’s struggles continue (0-5, 5.47 ERA).</p><p>David Sandlin has impressed with a 0.75 ERA in four Triple-A starts, while <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/24/white-sox-pitching-prospect-hagan-smith-munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-will-venable-brooks-baldwin-anthony-kay" target="_blank" ><u>Hagen Smith</u></a>, the Sox’ next top pitching prospect after Noah Schultz, has posted a 4.54 ERA in 10 starts.</p><p>“For him, it’s how he stacks over his back leg,” Sox pitching director Brian Bannister said. “If we get the lower body right, the stack right and he doesn’t feel stuck in that back leg, it’s pretty electric on how many guys he can strike out.”</p><h3>Shane Smith on the mend</h3><p>Shane Smith, the Sox’ Opening Day starter who got demoted to Triple-A and then landed on the injured list with a rotator cuff injury, is expected to resume his throwing program in June.</p><p>The Sox’ 2025 All-Star stumbled out of the gate and didn’t look <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/24/demoted-starter-shane-smith-showing-improvement-in-charlotte" target="_blank" ><u>all that much better</u></a> at Charlotte, pitching to a 5.27 ERA in four starts before going down with the injury.</p><p>“He’s getting ready to start kind of the throwing program and working back towards being back on the starter’s schedule,” Janish said. “He’s doing well, progressing as he’s supposed to and he should be, at some point in June, back in the mix and in a normal role.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago Latinos 'show up and show out' at first Sueños since Operation Midway Blitz targeted communities
entries.summary: <p>This year Sueños Music Festival took place after Chicago saw one of its largest immigration enforcement operations in recent history.</p><p>But at Sueños on Sunday, Chicagoans showed up showcasing their Latino identity, waving flags, sporting cowboy boots and hats and singing along to songs in Spanish. Several said the weekend music event — one of the largest Latino music festivals in the country — offered them an opportunity to “show up and show out” and celebrate in hopes of something better.</p><p>Last fall, Chicago and its surrounding suburbs were the target of immigration officials in a campaign the feds named “Operation Midway Blitz.”</p><p>Latino residents endured weeks of targeted operations and detentions based on their identity, skin color, accent or occupation.</p><p>Fast forward five months, and the two-day music festival Sueños hosted attendees for its fifth year to see headliners such as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2026/05/24/suenos-music-festival-day-1-j-balvin-kali-uchis-danny-ocean" target="_blank" ><u>J Balvin and Kali Uchis</u></a>.</p><p>In Chicago, the Latino population is predominantly Mexican. That was in full display on Sunday, where the headliner was popular regional Mexican banda Fuerza Regida.</p><p>Here’s what some festivalgoers told us about returning to Sueños this year.</p><div entries.title: Mya shows crowd at Forever Mine that she is still the queen of the dance break
entries.summary: <p>After putting on a polished show of dynamic dancing, angelic vocals and charming stage presence on day two of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/23/forever-mine-festival-brings-y2k-nostalgia-and-chicago-house-culture-to-union-park" >Forever Mine Festival,</a> Mya called on Chicagoans to help her with a very special task.</p><p>“I’m searching tonight for a vegan deep dish spot,” the singer said backstage at the event, which was held at Union Park in West Loop. "I’ve been craving it all week.”</p><p>Mya’s appreciation for Chicago runs deep. Beyond name-dropping other local favorites like Garrett Popcorn, she also expressed her admiration of the iconic Chosen Few Picnic and House Music Festival, which she has hosted in the past. She praised the city’s house DJs for inspiring her; hometown hero DJ Terry Hunter has even remixed one of her songs.</p><p>“I love this city,” she said. “Not so much in the winter, but the summer has always been the season for me here. entries.title: Family visits generations laid to rest at Bohemian National Cemetery for Memorial Day: Photos
entries.summary: <p>Bob Kucaba, 70, stood with his sister Kathy and 94-year-old mother, Arlene, at Bohemian National Cemetery Sunday afternoon after sticking four roses into the ground in front of a headstone bearing their last name.</p><p>Visiting the site where Bob and Kathy’s father — Anton Kucaba, a World War II veteran and Bronze Star recipient — is buried alongside his father, mother and great-aunt at the North Park cemetery is a Memorial Day tradition the family has carried on for decades. After Anton died in 2018, they continued as usual, now with one more loved one to visit.</p><p>He had been a medic’s assistant in the Pacific theater and earned the award for dragging an injured man away from combat. He took after his elder brother before him, who was an ambulance driver in World War I.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-800000" name="image-800000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b888eaa/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5399x3030+0+285/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff6%2F50%2Fba000d3f41dabec0bd5f062dd7d0%2Fmemorialdaycemeteries-260525-003.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c508845/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5399x3030+0+285/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff6%2F50%2Fba000d3f41dabec0bd5f062dd7d0%2Fmemorialdaycemeteries-260525-003.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0f021a8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5399x3030+0+285/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff6%2F50%2Fba000d3f41dabec0bd5f062dd7d0%2Fmemorialdaycemeteries-260525-003.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Anton V. He is buried alongside his father, mother and great-aunt.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It could’ve been somebody else, but it was him,” Bob said of his father.</p><p>In 1973, they visited one of his father’s army friends in Bodega Bay — the filming location of Alfred Hitchcock’s “The Birds” — when he learned his father had once fallen asleep while taking enemy shell fire.</p><p>“He could fall asleep just like that,” he said.</p><p>But their family ties to the site go beyond that, as elsewhere in the cemetery, underneath a washed-out, limestone headstone Bob can no longer find, are his great-great-grandparents and other relatives as well.</p><p>The site was a popular spot for Czech families who came to the city in the 19th century, in addition to having extended family they’ve since lost touch with as the family tree branched further and further.</p><p>“It’s not the most common name, but there’s quite a number of us here,” Bob said. “The carvings of the names are hard to read. It’s been about 15 years; I’m not sure where it is anymore.”</p>

entries.title: Cubs approaching another historic feat as skid hits eight with loss to Astros
entries.summary: <p>The Cubs are streaking toward more history this season, but this time, it’s the bad kind.</p><p>After winning 10 games in a row twice in a season for the first time in franchise history since 1935, the Cubs are close to joining a select group of teams in baseball history that have won <i>and</i> lost 10 games in a row in the same season.</p><p>With their 8-5 loss to the Astros on Sunday, the Cubs have dropped eight in a row, falling from a season-high 15 games over .500 on May 8 to five. It’s their longest skid since a nine-game streak in July 2022. They lost 10 in a row in June that year.</p><p>With two more losses, the Cubs would become the 25th team with double-digit winning and losing streaks in a season, according to SABR. The Guardians did it last season, winning 10 straight and losing 10 straight.</p><p>The Astros could’ve been a tonic for the Cubs’ sickly offense, which scored more than three runs for the first time in a week. The Astros’ pitching staff has the worst ERA in the majors at 5.17, but the Cubs scored only seven runs in the series. Starter Peter Lambert, who rehabbed his career in Japan last season after failing with the Rockies, had one bad inning Sunday.</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell used another new lineup Sunday, adding shortstop Dansby Swanson to the bench along with left fielder Ian Happ, who also sat out Saturday. Swanson’s absence meant Pedro Ramirez, who was called up Friday, would make his first major-league start. He started at second base, with Nico Hoerner moving to short.</p><p>It was Ramirez, the club’s No. 2 prospect, who gave the offense life with his first big-league hit, a first-pitch double in the second inning that drove in the Cubs’ first run. Ramirez had debuted Saturday as a pinch hitter, admitting he was nervous playing before such a big crowd. He got over it.</p><p>“Good at-bats. That’s the big thing,” Counsell said of Ramirez, who worked a walk in his next plate appearance. “He came up in a number of big spots. The double was a big spot to get us on the board. Even the at-bat in the eighth [when he hit into a double play], he scorched the ball. Proud of Pedro; had a really nice game.”</p><p>But it’s not a good sign when an untested rookie is the one delivering in the clutch. Nico Hoerner went 1-for-5, watching his batting average drop from a season-high .342 to .255. Alex Bregman went 1-for-4 and is hitting .250. Neither has been producing commensurate with their nine-figure contracts.</p><p>The Cubs were a bit unlucky Sunday, hitting some balls hard but into outs. Astros shortstop Jeremy Pena put on a show, too, with several fine plays. In fact, according to Baseball Savant, the Cubs’ expected batting average for the game was .289 compared to the Astros’ .199. Michael Busch, batting .230, hit a two-run homer. So maybe the offense is coming around.</p><p>Still, it’s hard to put a positive spin on eight straight losses.</p><p>“Obviously, [we’re] just not playing good baseball in all phases,” Bregman said. “It comes down to execution, and we’ve been outexecuted the last eight days in a row. We’ve got to make an adjustment. It starts with me. Too many empty plate appearances. Got to be better.”</p><p>“You’ve gotta keep the faith,” Happ told the Sun-Times. “At some point, this will look like a blip. We’re going to win a lot of baseball games this year. We’re still five games above .500. It’s been quite a roller coaster to get to that. When you rattle off two 10-game win streaks, that’s part of it. There’s gonna be some tough moments.”<br></p>

entries.title: After putting Edward Cabrera on injured list, Cubs watch Shota Imanaga struggle again
entries.summary: <p>Sunday wasn’t a good day for Cubs starting pitchers.</p><p>In the morning, the team put Edward Cabrera on the 15-day injured list because of the blister on his right middle finger that forced him from his last start Wednesday. In the afternoon, Shota Imanaga had a second consecutive rough outing, allowing seven runs, including three home runs, in six innings in the Cubs’ 8-5 loss to the Astros.</p><p>The Cubs’ rotation is already short-staffed, with Matthew Boyd (left knee) on the 15-day IL, Justin Steele (left elbow) shut down and Cade Horton (right forearm) out for the season. In fact, the only good news with the unit was that Boyd’s recovery “is going very well,” according to manager Craig Counsell. But he still has about three weeks to go.</p><p>Cabrera still was affected by the blister during a bullpen session Sunday.</p><p>“It’s just still there, is the best way to say it,” Counsell said. “The more he stepped on a pitch, the more he felt it. We’re optimistic this could be a minimum or very close to a minimum stint. But we just got to let that hot area cool down, so to speak.”</p><p>The Cubs called up Jordan Wicks from Triple-A Iowa, where he had a 4.44 ERA in seven starts, covering 26 ⅓ innings. In his last three outings, though, Wicks allowed one run with 12 strikeouts in 15 innings. Counsell said he’ll be “involved” in the game Tuesday in Pittsburgh, which was Cabrera’s next start.</p><p>Imanaga, meanwhile, has allowed 15 earned runs in his last 10 ⅓ innings, including five homers. The big blow Sunday was a three-run homer by Christian Walker, his third homer of the series, in the Astros’ five-run fifth. Imanaga threw his trademark splitter, but he has been struggling with it lately.</p><p>“He made a mistake to a dangerous hitter in a spot where [there’s] not a lot of space to pitch around him,” Counsell said. “Three-run homers are tough to overcome.”</p><p>“In the beginning, [the splitter] felt good,” Imanaga said, “but in the later innings, it felt like the splitters that were trying to go down below the zone were left up in the zone. The best ones are when it starts in the bottom of the zone and drops to the hitters’ knees. That’s something I need to work on.”</p><p>The Cubs have now allowed 73 home runs, the second-most in the majors.</p><p>“We’ve got to prevent homers better,” Counsell said. “If you give up the number of homers we’re giving up, that’s a problem.”</p><p>So is the health of the starting pitchers whom the Cubs expected to have entering the season.</p><p>“Injuries to the pitching side are going to be part of the season,” Counsell said. “We've got to withstand that, as we have some other stretches. We’ve got two guys [Boyd and Cabrera] coming back in probably two-ish, three-ish weeks. Certainly, some guys are going to have opportunities in the meantime.”<br></p>

entries.title: Cubs' Ian Happ trying to keep level head after two-game benching
entries.summary: <p>Cubs left fielder Ian Happ is trying to keep a level head after being benched for the second consecutive game Sunday.</p><p>“That’s the hard part,” Happ told the Sun-Times after the Cubs lost to the Astros 8-5 for their eighth consecutive defeat. “[It’s] really to focus on your process and your work and what you’re trying to accomplish.</p><p>“It’s a team sport, so everybody’s going through it together and feeling the frustration and bringing that positive attitude every day, and you’re understanding that this thing isn’t gonna last. We’re gonna win a series and get rolling.”</p><p>It would help if Happ got rolling. His batting average has plummeted to .214, second-lowest among Cubs regulars behind shortstop Dansby Swanson, who also was given Sunday off. Manager Craig Counsell told Happ on Saturday not to even pick up a bat. Happ did some work Sunday and said the time off was “productive.”</p><p>“Sometimes it’s good to just watch nine innings and have a reset,” Happ said. “I was ready to come into the game [Sunday]. You don’t get any days to work without playing, so having a couple days to work on the swing is nice.”</p><p>“He’ll be back in there [Monday in Pittsburgh],” Counsell said. “I thought two days was best for Ian right here.”</p><p>Happ said he isn’t thinking about his contract status. He’s in the last season of a three-year, $61 million contract, and he has seen the Cubs give Pete Crow-Armstrong and Nico Hoerner nine-figure deals this year.</p><p>“No. You’re so focused on the process and what you’re going through,” Happ said. “That stuff works itself out when it does.”<br></p>

entries.title: Sueños’ Sunday lineup an ode to Mexican Regional music with Fuerza Regida, Los Tucanes de Tijuana
entries.summary: <p>Perhaps the only artist to make almost every single attendee in Grant Park dance in unison, Los Tucanes de Tijuana brought their classic song “La Chona” to Chicago’s fifth annual Sueños Music Festival on Sunday evening. Performing on the main stage for a “special performance,” the norteño-genre veterans drew a truly multigenerational crowd on Day 2 of the Memorial Day weekend event.</p><p>Sunday’s Sueños lineup was an ode to Mexican Regional music, with the great majority of artists in the lineup identifying as Mexican immigrants or Mexican Americans. For local residents, the significance of the artist selection was not lost on them after Chicago and the surrounding suburbs were targets of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign Midway Blitz last year. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/24/suenos-music-festival-midway-blitz-latino-mexican-celebration-joy-fuerza-regida" target="_blank" ><u>Latinos came to the fest over the weekend “to show up and show out,”</u></a> proudly representing their cultures.</p><p>The spectrum of banda and norteño music has been topping Billboard, Spotify, Apple and Amazon Music charts for multiple consecutive years, as showcased by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2025/05/24/peso-pluma-returns-to-chicagos-suenos-festival-with-a-crowd-pleasing-set" target="_blank" ><u>last year’s popular Peso Pluma performance</u></a> at Sueños. Even so, the Trump administration has implemented changes that tighten restrictions on the visa process, with artists based in Mexico having reportedly experienced denials or challenges to perform in the United States.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> mascot, “El Chuyín.”</p><p>The daytime highlights were Kane Rodriguez with his trending song “Se Volvieron Locos,” while the popular singer-songwriter Chino Pacas sang shirtless for half of his set and invited a fan from the crowd onstage. He later made a guest appearance with Fuerza Regida, where they sang “Que Onda.”</p><p>While Los Tucanes de Tijuana interpreted the classically composed corridos that many immigrants grew up with — with themes of rancho life, migration, work and family — Fuerza Regida embodied the modern lyrics and musical taste of the bilingual children of immigrants who, as adults, are making Mexican music go global.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2026/05/23/suenos-music-festival-kicks-off-in-grant-park-j-balvin-kali-uchis" >Sueños Music Festival kicks off in Grant Park, celebrating Latin music and culture</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2026/05/24/suenos-music-festival-day-1-j-balvin-kali-uchis-danny-ocean" >Sueños Day 1: J Balvin returns to Grant Park to mark fest’s fifth anniversary</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/24/suenos-music-festival-midway-blitz-latino-mexican-celebration-joy-fuerza-regida" >Chicago Latinos ‘show up and show out’ at first Sueños since Operation Midway Blitz targeted communities</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/25/kaytranada-monica-forever-mine-union-park-chicago-music-festival-summer" >Kaytranada and Monica close out Chicago’s first Forever Mine fest, celebrating long legacy of R&B</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Kaytranada and Monica close out Chicago’s first Forever Mine fest, celebrating long legacy of R&B
entries.summary: <p>As the sun set on Union Park on Sunday, a Forever Mine festival attendee from Canada exclaimed, “I’ve been waiting since grade 9 for this!”</p><p>She was referring to Kaytranda, who, along with Monica, headlined day two of the inaugural festival in Union Park dedicated to R&B and house music. Shaggy was originally slated as a third headliner, but was removed from the schedule without explanation, prompting one too many “it wasn’t him” jokes based on his 2000 hit single.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/23/forever-mine-festival-brings-y2k-nostalgia-and-chicago-house-culture-to-union-park" target="_blank" ><u>Day one of the event,</u></a> led by Keyshia Cole, Kelly Rowland and Juvenile, appeared to go off without a hitch.</p><p>The excited Kaytranada fan said the Haitian-Canadian producer, 33, had a knack for picking the perfect R&B singers for his electronic dance beats. She was right; he played a vigorous set of songs featuring Syd, Rochelle Jordan, Kali Uchis (who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suenos-music-festival/2026/05/24/suenos-music-festival-day-1-j-balvin-kali-uchis-danny-ocean" target="_blank" ><u>headlined the nearby Sueños Music Festival</u></a> the night prior), Teedra Moses, Victoria Monet and Chicago’s own <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/07/30/ravyn-lenae-chicago-high-school-arts-lollapalooza-sabrina-carpenter" target="_blank" ><u>Ravyn Lenae</u></a>. He not only embodied the fest’s tagline, “where R&B and house fall in love,” but served as the perfect act to bridge generations.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div youths, but Kaytranada beckoned a younger crowd to celebrate the long legacy of Black music.</p><p>“You know I always gotta come back here,” said Kaytranada, who also made kissing noises to the audience. “I love y’all and I appreciate y’all.”</p><p>Clearly a serious student of his predecessors, the producer is both a nerd and the life of the party. A hip-hop head, Kaytranda played his songs featuring a variety of rappers, from Phonte to Childish Gambino. He showed off some impressive moves while DJing, sliding, twerking, kicking, posing and even doing push-ups onstage. He nearly sent the crowd into a frenzy when he removed his jacket at one point.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a A different fan seemed surprised and excited by how well he kept her attention.</p><p>“He doesn’t even sing!” she screamed multiple times.</p><p>Kaytranada was preceded by Monica, who had a more subdued, though no less entertaining set. Before delivering an emotional rendition of her hit “Angel of Mine,” she shared some heartbreaking news about her ill father.</p><p>“The doctor says there’s nothing else they can do for my dad,” she told the crowd. But she said she didn’t want to miss the show and disappoint the festival-goers because “y’all showed up for all of us.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Dear Abby: Man who abandoned family reappears after 16 years
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I was married for 39 years to "Morris," an alcoholic and a spendthrift. In 2010, he announced he was having an affair with his boss, and the next day he moved in with and eventually married her. I was left filled with anger and resentment, and so were my two grown boys. Eventually, we realized what a toxic environment it had been and accepted hearing from him only twice a year or so.</p><p>A few months ago, Morris' wife died, and he has been wanting to be "friends" and a "family" again. He has no friends and has been retired more than 10 years. None of us wants to be that involved again (though he has been in AA for 10 years), but my older son, "Justin," has begrudgingly become the recipient of his father's multiple daily texts and emails.</p><p>Morris is lonely and depressed. We have told him to go to counseling, volunteer, take classes, etc., and Justin and I have tried to set limits. Justin just got married and wants to share the burden of their dad, but my younger son hasn't communicated much with Morris. Justin's wife doesn't want Morris to disrupt their lives. Unfortunately, Morris now wants to move closer to them.</p><p>This whole mess is causing a rift between the boys. Any suggestions on how we all can handle this situation? — <i>WEARY IN FLORIDA</i></p><p><b>DEAR WEARY:</b> Tell your sons they are not responsible for Morris, who deserted you all for greener pastures. (Please note that I did not refer to him as their father.) You and your sons are not responsible for causing the depression Morris is now experiencing. If he needs emotional support, he can get it at the nearest AA meeting. Please do not allow him to disrupt your lives any further than he has already. Unless your recently married son disengages with Morris, it could create a serious disruption in his marriage.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My daughter has successfully divorced her husband on paper. However, he is still living at her house. They have two beautiful children together, and he has two from a prior marriage who stay with them three nights a week. She feels bad that he doesn't have a place to go. He wants to buy a house, but he spends all his money. We offered a downpayment, but our daughter will not allow it. How can we encourage her to set a deadline for the ex to move out? — <i>HELPING THEM MOVE ON</i></p><p><b>DEAR HELPING:</b> I have a thought. If you want him out of your daughter's house, invite him to stay with you "until he gets settled." And while you are at it, encourage your daughter to discuss the living arrangements currently in place with her attorney in case she may be incurring any financial liabilities by having him continue to live under her roof.</p><p><b>DEAR READERS:</b> Along with the millions of Americans who are observing this Memorial Day, I'm adding my prayer of thanks for those courageous men and women who have sacrificed their lives in service to our country. May they rest in peace. — <i>LOVE, ABBY</i></p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Good advice for everyone — teens to seniors — is in "The Anger in All of Us and How to Deal With It." To order, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Anger Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Redefining 'Trump Derangement Syndrome'
entries.summary: <p>We need to correctly identify who really suffers from "Trump Derangement Syndrome."</p><p>The term shouldn't apply to those who vehemently oppose Donald Trump. Rather, it is an appropriate description for his ride or dies.</p><p>If you support a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/05/30/trump-guilty-first-us-president-convicted-felony-crimes" >34-count convicted felon</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/1/12/22227269/trump-impeachment-capitol-riot-second" target="_blank" >twice impeached</a> president, you have TDS.</p><p>If you think Trump cares about the middle class and our struggles with the higher prices of goods and service since he took office, you have TDS.</p><p>If you think as commander-in-chief, he knows what the hell he’s doing in the Middle East besides enriching himself, you have TDS.</p><p>If you think Trump is charitable by <a class="Link" href="https://finance.yahoo.com/news/trump-says-gets-no-credit-133500907.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAAM13Z29-ixMR8ocuMxyc5cDzPb-OriNFZESRcSxyQcgf8QF0MFbdqVPgdiQ9tf7gPAE2LhG-xe1oZZMDLKgduUsp8zhxhtfLR1TobN2BUnYln-N1V5rHIGPRK2eSxblahmfu-O2BgHhNfMJJmDbL5vU7T5hoJk8T6_CbSN9kI571" target="_blank" >“waiving”</a> his presidential salary all the while making billions of dollars from merchandise, <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/how-trumps-500-million-uae-crypto-deal-trades-u-s-national-security-for-family-profit/" target="_blank" >cryptocurrency</a> and other scams, you have TDS.</p><p>Trump said <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/30/politics/fact-check-trump-mexico-piece-border-wall" target="_blank" >Mexico was going to pay</a> for the wall. He said the new ballroom was going to <a class="Link" href="https://www.democrats.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/in-their-own-words-after-trump-said-taxpayers-wouldnt-pay-one-dime-for-his-ballroom-republicans-move-to-stick-them-with-a-1-billion-bill" target="_blank" >cost taxpayers</a> nothing.</p><p>The man is stealing from the American people right in front of our faces. If you deny that he's ripping us off, you have TDS.</p><p>Wake up.</p><p>Trump and his sycophants are destroying our country and our standing in the world. We need to put a stop to this overt corruption. For those of us who don't suffer from TDS and those in recovery: Vote in November, and take back Congress from the Republicans. Impeach, convict and remove this corrupt, criminal president!</p><p><i>William Coyne, Schererville, Indiana</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-340000" name="module-340000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Driverless car concerns</h3><p>Two delivery robots shattered CTA <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/03/24/delivery-robot-goes-viral-after-shattering-west-town-bus-shelter-glass" >bus shelters’ glass</a> in March. Scientists' explanation of these incidents — "<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/05/06/delivery-robots-chicago-crashes-damage" target="_blank" >edge cases</a>" — was reported recently in the Sun-Times.</p><p>Technology has bugs — that's normal. The problem is deploying technologies into public space before deciding what an acceptable bug looks like. The higher the stakes, the less we can afford to wait.</p><p>For a delivery robot, an edge case is a broken bus shelter. For a 3-ton driverless Waymo navigating a Chicago winter, an edge case is worse. Robotaxis have not been meaningfully tested in our snow, slush and black ice. There is no public plan for what happens when they encounter a January morning on Lake Shore Drive. Springfield is nonetheless considering <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/02/26/kam-buckner-three-year-test-self-driving-vehicles-illinois-waymo" >pending legislation</a> that would greenlight deployment without adequate plans in place.</p><p>The unanswered questions extend beyond weather. The rideshare industry employs thousands of Chicago-area residents whose wages support families and neighborhoods.</p><p>No plan exists for how those workers transition as a $100-billion-plus industry, built on public roads, data and subsidy, eliminates their jobs by design. No plan exists for how an industry that profits from removing labor will contribute to keeping Chicago the most affordable big city in the country. No plan exists, full stop.</p><p>These tech giants have given Chicago-area residents reasons to doubt their intentions. Waymo's parent company, Alphabet Inc., is also the parent company of Google, which is among the <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/23/trump-white-house-ballroom-donors" target="_blank" >top donors</a> to Donald Trump's ballroom project.</p><p>Tesla CEO Elon Musk was Trump's top campaign donor.</p><p>These are not the actors we should trust to write the rules for our infrastructure, jobs and public space. Our public officials need to put community safety and economic security first, rather than rolling over for these behemoths. We have leverage, and it's on our officials to set robust terms so this technology works for people — not just for corporations enabling authoritarianism.</p><p>Whether you call yourself a technologist, a capitalist, a socialist or something else, the premise is the same: Technology is not neutral. It carries the values of the people who build it and the rules of the places that let it operate. A delivery robot shattering a bus shelter is a warning. A robotaxi misreading a snowstorm — with no plan for the driver it just replaced — is a choice we can preempt.</p><p>Before opening the doors to autonomous vehicles, let's put safeguards in place for human lives, displaced workers and our public infrastructure.</p><p><i>Ishan Daya, Institute for the Public Good</i><br><i>Will Tanzman</i><b><i>,</i></b><i> The People’s Lobby</i></p><h3>Lack of commitment to education reprehensible</h3><p>Last year, 881 Lane Tech students took the Advanced Placement Government exam, achieving a staggering 93% pass rate. Because passing an AP exam earns college credit, those 820 passing students saved Chicago families roughly $1.23 million in tuition at universities like the University of Illinois.</p><p>Across the entire school, Lane administered over 7,200 exams — more than any other school in the nation — saving Chicago Public Schools families millions more.</p><p>When you factor in every AP and International Baccalaureate course, athletic program and mental health resource across all CPS, it is clear: No institution does more for the common good of our city than CPS.</p><p>Yet, the Chicago Board of Education claims it can't find<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/12/cps-plans-cut-teacher-positions-raise-class-sizes-shrink-723-million-deficit" > $700 million</a> to close its budget gap and prevent mass layoffs. Meanwhile, sports stars sign multi-million dollar contracts, billionaire team owners get fast-tracked tax breaks, and our federal government burns through billions on foreign conflicts.</p><p>We have endless funds for gladiators, coliseums and wars. But when it comes to educating children and lifting up working families, our political leaders cry "poor mouth."</p><p>The path our nation is on now reminds me of a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/02/03/opinion/abraham-lincoln-ambition-speech.html" target="_blank" >quote</a> from Abraham Lincoln: "If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher. As a nation of freemen we must live through all time or die by suicide." </p><p>By starving our public schools, our leaders are authorizing that exact destruction. Lane Tech AP Government students understand Lincoln's warning. Do our politicians?</p><p><i>Steve Parsons, teacher, Lane Tech High School</i></p>

entries.title: A Sun-Times reporter discovers 'Mr. Main's House,' an ancestor’s family retreat in China
entries.summary: <p>For most of my life, China existed in my family as a distant but persistent presence — a place spoken of in fragments, attached to old photos and diaries about a great-grandfather who spent decades there as an American missionary.</p><p>I have never visited China. I don’t speak Mandarin or Cantonese.</p><p>But my great-grandfather, William Artyn Main, considered China home for much of his life.</p><p>He arrived there in 1896, shortly after graduating from Northwestern University and marrying his wife, Emma.</p><p>Assigned to Methodist missions in Fuzhou, in southeastern China, he became treasurer of the church’s operations there.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-860000" name="module-860000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>He lived through political upheaval and war, remained during the Japanese invasion in 1937 and didn't leave permanently until 1941, when the conflict forced his evacuation. He died in California four years later, unable to return.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-700000" name="image-700000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6a03a53/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1172x658+0+438/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2Fc4%2F672067ac45acb2ac3710945222f1%2Fscreenshot-2026-05-20-at-10-46-33-pm.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3a1ad98/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1172x658+0+438/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2Fc4%2F672067ac45acb2ac3710945222f1%2Fscreenshot-2026-05-20-at-10-46-33-pm.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7928676/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1172x658+0+438/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F26%2Fc4%2F672067ac45acb2ac3710945222f1%2Fscreenshot-2026-05-20-at-10-46-33-pm.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A Chicago Daily Tribune story lists Northwestern University graduates feared dead in the Boxer rebellion in China in 1900. William A. Main and his family spent their summers in Kuliang, a mountain community in the hills outside the big city of Fuzhou.</p><p>Kuliang is known for its cooler climate and lush landscape.</p><p>I'd never enough on its own. But there was more.</p><p>Through conversations with his Chinese contacts, Thomas learned about the “Friends of Kuliang,” a group made up largely of descendants of American missionaries who once lived there. Some have returned to visit and formed enduring relationships with local residents.</p><p>Over the years, Kuliang has also become a symbolic site of cultural exchange between China and the United States, hosting student performances and other events encouraged by Xi and his wife.</p><p>Part of that effort traces back to 1992, when Xi was serving as Communist Party chief in Fuzhou.</p><p>After reading about an American woman named Elizabeth Gardner, whose husband had spent part of his childhood in Kuliang and longed to see it again before he died, Xi arranged for her to visit the town.</p><p>Two decades later, while serving as China’s vice president, Xi recounted the episode during an official trip to the United States.</p><p>"I believe there are a lot of touching stories like entries.title: Pope Leo calls for robust regulation of AI in manifesto that ponders the future of humanity
entries.summary: <p>(AP) — <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/hub/pope-leo-xiv" target="_blank" >Pope Leo XIV</a> called Monday for robust regulation of artificial intelligence and for its developers to work for the common good rather than profit, issuing a sweeping manifesto on safeguarding humankind as the technology impacts everything from work to war.</p><p>“Magnifica Humanitas” (Magnificent Humanity), <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/vatican-artificial-intelligence-pope-musk-nvidia-trump-889c0066f0d5ce784c07abb72b33e24c" target="_blank" >Leo’s first encyclical</a>, has been eagerly awaited ever since history’s first U.S.-born pope announced days after his election that he considered AI to be the biggest challenge facing humanity today.</p><p>In the text, Leo denounced the “culture of power” driving the AI race, especially in developing ever more sophisticated methods of remote warfare. He declared that it was “not permissible” to entrust irreversible, lethal decisions to AI systems, setting up another flash point between the American pope and the Trump administration, which has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-ai-executive-order-ee318f35acc8a2c43e47f3ebf26cb459" target="_blank" >worked aggressively to deregulate AI development.</a></p><p>“Artificial Intelligence now demands to be disarmed, freed from logics that turn it into an instrument of domination, exclusion and death,″ the pope told a special Vatican presentation of the encyclical, one of the most authoritative types of teaching documents a pope can issue.</p><p>Experts in the tech industry, academia and Catholic morality said the document will likely become a benchmark in the debate over AI, a point of reference for policymakers, researchers and ordinary folk alike. It comes as the near-daily developments in the technology trigger concerns rise over AI replacing human jobs and even human intelligence.</p><p>“It lends itself to people who are at the forefront of these tools and able to see the incredible things that they’re able to do, to have questions about their own ‘What does it mean to be human?’” said Taylor Black, a Microsoft AI executive and director of Catholic University of America’s AI institute.</p><p><b>Pope calls out AI companies even as he hosts Anthropic</b></p><p>The Vatican launch also included remarks by the co-founder of Anthropic, which is currently locked in a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/ai-anthropic-trump-security-risk-a8cfd07b4d975ddfc5be7e016ed3ddce" target="_blank" >legal battle with the Trump administration</a> over access to its AI technology. The Vatican decided to involve Anthropic as part of its decade-long effort to engage Silicon Valley in dialogue over the human cost of AI.</p><p>And yet in his text, Leo repeatedly blasted the concentration of power and data in the hands of so few people in the private sector as a danger, especially to children and the most vulnerable, and called for external regulation of their work.</p><p>“It is not enough to invoke ethics in the abstract; robust legal frameworks, independent oversight, informed users and a political system that does not abdicate its responsibility are required,” he wrote. “A more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few.”</p><p>Leo appealed several times to AI developers and political leaders responsible for regulating them to just slow down and reflect on what they are doing. He urged them to use ethical and spiritual guidelines to make the choice to work not for their own profit or power, but the betterment of humanity.</p><p>AI competitors OpenAI and Anthropic are the second- and third-most valuable U.S. private companies, each valued at hundreds of billions of dollars, more than the GDP of many nations.</p><p>Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah welcomed Leo’s criticism and concern. He said such external checks on AI and the researchers behind it were fundamental to the technology “going well” for humankind since there is so much at stake — “a real possibility that AI will displace human labor at a very large scale.”</p><p>“We need more of the world — religious communities, civil society, scholars, governments — to do what His Holiness has done here: to take this seriously, to look closely, and to push events in a better direction,” Olah said. “We need informed critics who will tell the labs when we are failing. We need moral voices that the incentives cannot bend.”</p><p><b>Experts say the text will become a benchmark</b></p><p>In a methodical text, the math major pope traced the history of the Catholic Church’s social teaching and applied its core concepts — justice, solidarity, the dignity of work and the universal destination of resources — to the digital revolution.</p><p>“I am convinced that this will prove to be a defining document for our era, a profound and prophetic document,” said Paolo Carozza, law professor at Notre Dame Law School and chair of the Meta oversight board.</p><p>“Pope Leo is offering a clear, comprehensive, and coherent voice urging us to take responsibility for constructing a world in which technology will serve humans rather than degrade them,” he said.</p><p>In its strongest chapters, Leo denounced how AI had helped accelerate the “normalization of war” by desensitizing people to its cost. He didn’t name specific conflicts, but cited “opposing imperialisms, between powers that wish to preserve their supremacy, and those that aspire to seize that supremacy.”</p><p>He demanded transparency and accountability by AI developers so that the chain of decision-making command in ordering strikes with AI weaponry is always known. He declared that the Catholic Church’s “just war” theory, which provides specific criteria for when force can be justified, was now “outdated” given the technological advances of warfare.</p><p><b>A text in the church’s social justice tradition</b></p><p>Leo signed the text May 15, the 135th anniversary of the publication of “Rerum Novarum” (Of New Things), the most important teaching document of Leo’s hero and namesake, Pope Leo XIII. That document addressed workers’ rights, the limits of capitalism, and the obligations that states and employers owed workers as the Industrial Revolution was underway.</p><p>It became the foundation of modern Catholic social thought, and the current pope cited it at the start of his pontificate in relation to the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/artificial-intelligence-documentaries-sam-altman-8ed278203fce377199ea3eb93776c56c" target="_blank" >AI revolution</a>, which he believes poses the same existential questions that the Industrial Revolution posed over a century ago. “Magnifica Humanitas” thus becomes the latest chapter in a century-long history of popes adapting “Rerum Novarum” to the social questions of their times, often dwelling on the dignity of work for human flourishing.</p><p>AI is evoking both <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/artificial-intelligence-documentaries-sam-altman-8ed278203fce377199ea3eb93776c56c" target="_blank" >existential fears and utopian vision</a> amid an intensifying debate on whether it will become a catalyst that enriches humanity or a technological toxin that dulls human intelligence while wiping out millions of high-paying jobs.</p><p>“The pursuit of greater profits cannot justify choices that systematically sacrifice jobs, because the human person is an end, not a means, and the economic order must remain subordinate to human dignity and the common good,” Leo wrote.</p><p>Leo extended his concern for upholding human dignity in labor to issue the first-ever papal apology for the Holy See’s own <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pope-apologizes-slavery-role-holy-see-vatican-78df993c5604eb098b19f255b89b3155" target="_blank" >role in legitimizing slavery</a> by giving European sovereigns explicit authority to subjugate and enslave “infidels.”</p><p><b>A decade-long dialogue with Silicon Valley</b></p><p>Vatican officials declined to say who exactly contributed to Leo’s encyclical. But Vatican and church officials have been engaged in a dialogue with Silicon Valley tech firms for a decade. Toward the end of his pontificate, Pope Francis began <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pope-francis-ai-g7-italy-610b8f16aac4d36aa8a56c88de2ca09f" target="_blank" >speaking out more</a> about AI and the risks it poses to humanity.</p><p>The decision to include Anthropic at the Vatican launch was criticized by some who considered it a papal stamp of approval of the AI firm, which is currently suing the Trump administration after it ordered all U.S. agencies to <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/eb59a72f46996f765711d4262b1ed6c5" target="_blank" >stop using</a> Anthropic’s technology for its refusal to allow the U.S. military unrestricted use of it.</p><p>Brian Boyd, U.S. faith liaison for the nonprofit Future of Life Institute, read the inclusion of Anthropic’s co-founder Olah as similar to a papal audience with a head of state: not an endorsement.</p><p>“I think it’s more like a recognition of (how) this is an extremely powerful company that’s currently winning this race to replace human workers,” Boyd said.</p><p>Anthropic is an “enormous corporation that is taking onto itself an enormous risk and responsibility,” Boyd continued, but said the company has “demonstrated genuine goodwill and integrity and interest in dialogue.”</p>

entries.title: Toddler fatally shot himself in the head, man arrested
entries.summary: <p>A 2-year-old was fatally shot inside a Pullman home Sunday afternoon, and a 31-year-old man was arrested, Chicago police said.</p><p>Jamonte Shaw was at the home around 12:40 p.m. in the 900 block of East 104th Street when he shot himself in the head. </p><p>Jamonte, who lived in the same block, was taken in critical condition to Comer Children's Hospital but he was pronounced dead at 1:31 p.m., according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>No charges have been announced for the man, 31, who was arrested in connection to the shooting, police said.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man dies after plunging off bridge in Loop
entries.summary: <p>A man died after falling from a bridge in the Loop Sunday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Police and paramedics responded to a call in the 100 block of East Jackson Boulevard at 6:55 p.m. and found Fernando Velazquez Contreras, 31, unresponsive, according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Contreras, of the 1900 block of West 17th Street, was taken to Northwestern Hospital where he was pronounced dead at 7:25 p.m., according to the medical examiner's office. </p><p>An autopsy is scheduled. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man accused of gunning down 74-year-old man in Auburn Gresham
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged in the fatal shooting of a 74-year-old man in Auburn Gresham Friday, according to Chicago</p><p>Elijah Winsley, 20, faces a charge of murder, police said. He was arrested hours after the shooting took place about a mile away from the scene.</p><p>A motive was not given for the shooting attack that unfolded as the 74-year-old was inside a residence in the 8100 block of South Laflin Street — the same block where Winsley lives — about 1:30 p.m. Friday, Chicago police said. </p><p>The man, whose name was not being released pending notification of relatives, was hit twice and was taken to Advocate Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn, where he was pronounced dead, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Winsley is due in court Monday.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Teen missing from Uptown
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old who may be in need of medical attention has gone missing from the Uptown neighborhood, police say. </p><p>Saphyrion Whitmore, 16, was last seen Tuesday, May 19, in the 4400 block of North Clark Street, police said. </p><p>Whitmore stands about 5-foot-2, is about 130 pounds, and has brown eyes and black hair, police said. Whitmore's race was listed as unknown in a statement by police. </p><p>Anyone with information should contact Area 3 special victim's unit, 312-744-8266. </p>

entries.title: White Sox promote Japanese prospect Rikuu Nishida from Charlotte before Twins game Monday
entries.summary: <p>As expected, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> promoted infielder/outfielder Rikuu Nishida from Triple-A Charlotte before Monday’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/24/white-sox-500-momentum-san-francisco-seattle-road-trip" target="_blank" >game</a> against the Twins, giving Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami a fellow countryman on the team’s roster. </p><p>Nishida, 25, is batting ninth and playing right field. In a corresponding move, outfielder Jarred Kelenic was designated for assignment.<br> <br>Nishida, from Osaka, is slashing.347/.454/.395 (43-124) with three doubles, one home run, 10 RBI, 21 walks, nine stolen bases, 33 runs and an .849 OPS over 33 games with Charlotte this season since being promoted from Double-A Birmingham on April 17. The 5-foot-6, 150-pound Nishida has appeared in 24 games at second base, 10 in right field, three in left and two in center with the Knights.</p><p>Nishida is batting a combined .323/.449/.384 (53-164) with seven doubles, one homer, 12 RBI, 32 RBI, 15 stolen bases, 43 runs scored and an .833 OPS over 44 games between Birmingham and Charlotte in 2026. <br></p>

entries.title: Latinos de Chicago 'hacen acto de presencia y se lucen' en el primer Festival Sueños desde el Operativo Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>Este año, el Festival Sueños se llevó a cabo después de que Chicago presenció uno de sus operativos migratorios más grandes de la historia reciente.</p><p>Pero el domingo en Sueños, los residentes de Chicago se presentaron mostrando su identidad latina, ondeando banderas, luciendo botas y sombreros vaqueros y cantando canciones en español. Varios dijeron que el evento musical del fin de semana —uno de los festivales de música latina más grandes del país— les ofreció una oportunidad para "hacer acto de presencia y lucirse" y para celebrar con la esperanza de que viene algo mejor.</p><p>El otoño pasado, Chicago y sus suburbios circundantes fueron el objetivo de los funcionarios de inmigración en una campaña que los federales llamaron "Operativo Midway Blitz".</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7f0000" name="module-7f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los residentes latinos soportaron semanas de operativos y detenciones dirigidas basadas en su identidad, color de piel, acento u ocupación.</p><p>Cinco meses después, el festival de música de dos días Sueños recibió a los asistentes en su quinto año para ver a artistas principales como <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/24/j-balvin-y-kali-uchis-regresan-a-grant-park-para-celebrar-el-quinto-aniversario-del-festival-suenos" target="_blank" >J Balvin y Kali Uchis</a>.</p><p>En Chicago, la población latina es predominantemente mexicana. Eso fue evidente el domingo, cuando el artista principal fue la popular banda regional mexicana Fuerza Regida.</p><p>Esto es lo que algunos asistentes al festival nos contaron sobre su regreso a Sueños este año.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e49be4" name="image-e49be4"></a> entries.title: At least 25 shot, including toddler killed, during holiday weekend violence citywide
entries.summary: <p>At least 25 people have been shot since Friday evening, a toddler fatally, during the Memorial Day holiday weekend citywide. </p><p>Though a 31-year-old man was arrested in shooting death of toddler, Jamonte Shaw, no charges have been announced by police as of Monday afternoon. </p><p>Jamonte was at the home around 12:40 p.m. Sunday in the 900 block of East 104th Street in Pullman when he shot himself in the head, police said. He was pronounced dead less than an hour later. A Monday autopsy was inconclusive as to the cause and manner of the toddler's death, pending a police investigation, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>In other non-fatal weekend shootings, most recently a 21-year-old man was driving a black car in the 4100 block of block of South Racine Avenue in the Back of the Yards neighborhood about 10:40 p.m. Sunday when an assailant in another car opened fire, hitting him. He was in good condition at a hospital. </p><p>At about 8:05 p.m. Sunday, a 33-year-old old man was also left in good condition after being shot in the 1700 block of North Laramie Avenue in Austin about 8 p.m. Sunday. </p><p>Other shootings since Friday at 5 p.m. left <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/24/17-people-shot-overnight-chicago" target="_blank" >at least 22 other people shot across the city. </a><br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Mayor speaks out after 5 CPD officers hurt while dispersing Near West Side crowd during 'teen takeover'
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson decried an early Sunday morning 'unauthorized large gathering' apparently involving teens that ended with a car veering into five Chicago police officers, injuring them, as they were dispersing the crowd on the Near West Side. </p><p>Police have not announced any charges Monday against the driver, 18, who was arrested.</p><p>"Unauthorized large gatherings can quickly become dangerous, and early this morning, after curfew hours, we saw that firsthand," the mayor posted on X Sunday night. </p><p>Johnson said the people who participated in violent behavior should be held accountable, but many people, including city leaders and community members, have a responsibility to look out for young people.</p><p>"I continue to call on parents and guardians to know where their children are and to help ensure they are safe and accounted for," Johnson said in a post on X. "There also must be accountability for the individuals who participated in the violent and reckless behavior."</p><p>The officers were on foot at around 3:20 a.m. in the 1200 block of South Loomis Street when a blue sedan hit them, according to Chicago police. The 18-year-old male driver then ran into a CPD car, a pole and a fence before coming to a stop.</p><p>Five officers were injured and taken to nearby hospitals in fair condition. The driver, who wasn't injured, was arrested and charges were pending. A weapon was found in the car, police said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Unauthorized large gatherings can quickly become dangerous, and early this morning, after curfew hours, we saw that firsthand. I am grateful to the officers who responded diligently to help keep people safe and relieved that the officers who were injured are in fair condition.…</p>— Mayor Brandon Johnson (@ChicagosMayor) <a href="https://twitter.com/ChicagosMayor/status/2058736082934526441?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: 'I don’t feel like I’m a major-leaguer': Rikuu Nishida humble despite successful debut with White Sox
entries.summary: <p>New White Sox infielder/outfielder Rikuu Nishida was skipping and chuckling through the team’s clubhouse, and on the field at the Rate before Monday’s 3-1 win over over the Minnesota Twins.</p><p>The 25-year-old native of Osaka, Japan had a lot to be happy about before and after the game.</p><p>The White Sox had just promoted him from Triple-A Charlotte and he made his major league debut – batting ninth and playing right field in the same lineup with countryman and slugger Munetaka Murakami.</p><p>The 5-foot-6,150-pound Nishida even giggled way through a pregame interview session with reporters in the dugout. He understands and speaks English, but interpreter Kenzo Yagi was at his side to provide precise translations.</p><p>“I’m really really happy, excited, but really nervous at the same time,” Nishida said via Yagi. “I still can’t believe it’s true right now, so a lot of butterflies inside me.</p><p>“I don’t feel like I’m a major-leaguer. I am still like in a very humble state at the moment.”</p><p>In the win, Nishida came through with his first hit, seven outfield put-outs and a run-saving throw to the plate in the second inning that gunned down the Twins Orlando Arcia.</p><p><b>Added Pressure</b></p><p>Nishida put a little extra pressure on himself. He’s wearing uniform No. 51, the same worn by Hall of Famer and Japanese legend Ichiro Suzuki.</p><p>“The number itself speaks a lot,” Nishida said. “It’s a really big number for me to be honest.</p><p>“I’m still a little bit unsure about, you know, whether I can wear it or not, but you know, I’m speechless. I can’t even put into words how much of a great player Ichiro is."</p><p>Nishida looks up to Murakami, too, suggesting the 26-year-old rookie slugger is a “captain” kind of player.</p><p>At 6-foot-2 and 213 pounds, Murakami’s stature and classic power-hitting style is a polar opposite from Nishida’s, who’s expected to spray the ball and use his speed in line with Ichiro’s approach.</p><p><b>Took College Route</b></p><p>The White Sox selected Nishida in the 11<sup>th</sup> round in 2023 when he played for the University of Oregon for one season. He broke into American baseball with two years with separate junior college teams in Washington State (Cowlitz) in 2021 and Massachusetts (Hyannis) in 2022.</p><p>Nishida tries to balance baseball with other elements of his life. It hasn’t been all fun, he noted. His mother passed away while he was playing college ball and it had a “really big effect on me and how I am as a person right now,” he said.</p><p>That personal loss didn’t affect his joy for the sport.</p><p>“I just love the game of baseball,” he said. “It’s not about money. It’s not about being a hobby. I just love to play.</p><p>“I think that really show who I am as a person. That’s why I think everybody sees me as an energetic person.</p><p>“I also can be kind of quiet too… if you want me to,” he added with a laugh.</p><p><b>The Other Move</b></p><p>To make room for Nishida on the roster, the Sox designated outfielder Jarred Kelenic for assignment. Kelenic hit .226 with one homer and four RBIs in 19 games.</p><p><b>First or not?</b></p><p>There are ample Japanese players and stars in the majors.</p><p>Nishida is the ninth player to have been born in Japan, then been drafted and make it to the majors, according to SportRadar.</p><p>However, he’s the first with a Japanese surname or given name. The rest, starting with Bobby Fenwick who was picked by the Sox in 1966, appear to be American citizens. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts also is on the list.</p><p>Nishida regards that only as a historical footnote, however.</p><p>“There’s not a lot of meaning into it, because I’m just the first person in the books,” he said. “There’s obviously a lot of great (Japanese) players out there."</p><p></p><p></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-c049c890-588d-11f1-a90c-4dac6e724f6a"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 776px;"><br></td></tr></tbody></table><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Rikuu Nishida has impressive debut as White Sox top Twins
entries.summary: <p>Munetaka Murakami provided an early blast. Then Japanese countryman Rikuu Nishida added a timely, flashy assist from right field in his major-league debut to help the White Sox hold off the Minnesota Twins 3-1 on Monday at the Rate.</p><p>Murakami launched his 18<sup>th</sup> home run in the first inning, an arching solo shot off Zebby Matthews to right field that ended the slugger’s seven-game longball drought. He hadn’t gone deep since hitting two for the first time in his career on May 16 against the Cubs.</p><p>Murakami swatted the first pitch he saw, a high, inside fastball, on a 41-degree angle. It tied the game at 1 before a juiced-up announced crowd of 30,114.</p><p>Murakami usually talks to reporters after homering, but this time, he deferred attention to Nishida, who made immediate impact after being called up from Triple-A Charlotte before the game.</p><p>“It went really fast,” Nishida said to reporters in English in the clubhouse after the game.</p><p>The Osaka native grounded a single up the middle in the fourth for his first hit after striking out swinging in his first at-bat on a 1-for-3 afternoon </p><p>What the 5-foot-6, 150-pound Nishida did in the field was more electric.</p><p>He made seven putouts. Even better, Nishida cut down Orlando Arcia at the plate for the third out in the top of the second as Arcia tried to score from second on Alex Jackson’s single to right.</p><p>Nishida charged the ball and uncorked a bullet to catcher Drew Romo, throwing so hard that his left shoe fell off.</p><p>Arcia danced wide and evaded a tag, but also missed the plate. Romo applied the tag for the final out before Arcia could dive back and touch up.</p><p>“I tried to find my shoes, and when I was looked up, (Arcia) was already out,” quipped Nishida, who got a game ball from his teammates. </p><p>The assist kept the game tied at 1, then Romo hit his fifth homer, a two-run-drive, in the bottom half of the second to put Chicago ahead 3-1 and for good.</p><p>"Especially in his debut, to make such a good throw on the money like that, that was impressive,” Romo said.</p><p>Among Nishida’s catches in right was one against the netting on Austin Martin’s foul fly to end the fifth with two runners on. He raced in to grab Luke Keaschall’s looper for the first out of the seventh, then narrowly missed hanging on following a longer run and a diving attempt on Jackson’s shallow pop with two outs.</p><p>Jackson was credited with a double, but reliever Grant Taylor fanned Byron Buxton to end the threat.</p><p>“It was hard to see (flyballs), said Nishida, who has played mostly at second base in the minors. “I feel like it was the first time I played in a big stadium like that, so it was hard to read."</p><p>The win moved the White Sox back over .500, to 27-26, and kept them in second place in the AL Central, 1 ½ games ahead of Minnesota. The Twins entered on a four game winning streak and having won six of seven.</p><p>Sox starter Anthony Kay allowed a solo shot to Minnesota’s Brooks Lee in the first, but settled in and won for the third time in his last four starts to improve to 4-1. The left-hander allowed five hits and  one walk while striking out five.</p><p>Over his last four starts, Kay has yielded five runs and 15 hits in in 22 1/3 innings to trim his ERA to 3.96 after it peaked at 6.11 on April 27.</p><p>“I knew I always had it in me,” Kay said.“Kind of a rough start to the season. Just having that conviction is massive."</p><p>Kay relied heavily on his sweeper, one of six pitches in his repertoire, against the Twins. “It was probably my best strike pitch today,” he said.</p><p>The bullpen came through, with Taylor, Bryan Hudson and closer Seranthony Dominguez throwing a scoreless inning each</p><p>Dominguez pitched the ninth for his 11<sup>th</sup> save, but it wasn’t drama-free.  He appeared to have walked pinch hitter Tristan Gray leading off, but his sixth pitch – originally called a ball – was overturned to strike following Romo’s ABS challenge and Gray was called out.<br></p>
