entries.title: Sky banking on better ball movement to revive offense
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> had a nice long film session to start practice Monday.</p><p>Coming off two straight losses at home, coach Tyler Marsh had plenty of material to work with.</p><p>Like all those missed shots.</p><p>The Sky (3-3) are struggling to shoot, hitting 41.6% from the field and 27.1% from three-point range, both near the bottom of the WNBA. Marsh usually traces problems   on offense back to ball movement, which he has seen slow down since the Sky’s 3-1 start on the road.</p><p>“I think over the course of the first several games, we were really good at that, and we’ve gotten stagnant over the last couple,” Marsh said. “It hasn’t been for long durations, but it’s been at important moments.”</p><p>Marsh knows quick shots and iso-lation plays won’t turn the offense around, especially now that leading scorer and shot creator Rickea Jackson is out for the season after tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in her left knee.</p><p>But some of the shooting woes <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/07/the-sky-built-a-deeper-roster-and-tyler-marsh-isnt-worried-about-its-quirks" >were predictable given the roster.</a> The Sky added many great downhill drivers this past offseason, but few sharpshooters. Their top free-agent addition, Skylar Diggins, is a perfect example. She can blow by defenders with her speed and skill set, but she's only a career 41.9% shooter and is shooting 39% to start the year.</p><p>Marsh, of course, doesn’t believe the Sky are doomed to poor percentages. He thinks his system can generate clean looks, and he trusts players such as Diggins to knock down threes when they matter most.</p><p>“We’re generating open [shots] — we just haven’t knocked them down yet,” he said of the three-point shooting. “We expect that number to turn.”</p><p>A hot streak from Diggins would certainly help. So would stronger shoot-ing from veteran guard Rachel Banham, the Sky’s only player with a career three-point percentage above 35%.</p><p>But until <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/17/courtney-vandersloot-is-getting-really-close-to-returning" >the team is fully healthy</a>, the fate of the offense might rest on whether young starters Gabriela Jaquez and Jacy Sheldon can get back to where they began.</p><p>Both guards were efficient in the Sky’s hot start. Sheldon has since cooled off, scoring seven points combined over the last two games. And Jaquez, the rookie whose teammates say she’s already playing like a veteran, had her first rookie-ish performance Saturday against the Lynx. She shot 1-for-8, missing lay-ups she’d been making and forcing shots she’d usually leave alone.</p><p>The tough outing didn’t seem to faze her, though. After practice Monday, she sounded like a veteran once again.</p><p>“Watching the film today, we saw what we need to do,” Jaquez said. “But [it’s] also remembering we still have it in us. We see the good clips as well. It’s there. We’ve just got to do that more consistently. We have to create four quarters of consistent Chicago Sky basketball, and that will lead to wins.”</p><p>For now, the best aspect of Sky basketball has been their defense, which is still ranked in the top five in the league, despite some recent slippage. But the offense has strong points, too. The Sky rarely turn the ball over, which is a breath of fresh air after last season. They also get to the free-throw line more than almost any other WNBA team, with Jaquez, Diggins and center Kamilla Cardoso leading the way.</p><p>“We still believe in ourselves,” Jaquez said. “We’re still gonna be a great team. [It’s] just understanding how we have to adjust moving forward.”<br></p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Skid reaches nine as Cubs fall 2-1 in Pittsburgh
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — The uniformed cop came out of the visitors’ clubhouse shortly after the game ended Monday. Turns out he was on routine business.</p><p>At last check, the Pittsburgh PD hadn’t received an urgent request from Cubs chairman Tom Ricketts to open an investigation into his team’s missing bats.</p><p>Would anyone blame him if he did? This is not exactly the bang for his buck — tens of millions of them — Ricketts envisioned this season, especially after the Cubs ran off two 10-game winning streaks in the first 40 games.</p><p>The Cubs now have lost nine in a row after falling 2-1 to the Pirates before a Memorial Day crowd of 22,174 at PNC Park. The worm has turned and is lying in a hammock.</p><p>The Cubs’ only run came on a solo home run by Michael Busch in the fifth inning. They had only five other hits, all singles. Dansby Swanson chased a sweeper by Carmen Mlodzinski that was well off the plate with the bases loaded to end the second. Michael Conforto flied to left with two on to end the third.</p><p>Those were the Cubs’ only two at-bats with runners in scoring position. Meanwhile, Brandon Lowe doubled in a run against Cubs starter Ben Brown in the third, and .139-hitting catcher Henry Davis hit a tiebreaking homer against Trenton Thornton in the seventh.</p><p>The last 10 Cubs went down in order.</p><p>‘‘We’ve got to play better, we’ve got to pitch better, we need more guys contributing to good stuff and, as a coaching staff, we’ve got to figure out a way to get the players there,’’ manager Craig Counsell said. ‘‘Offensively, we are equipped to be way more consistent than this and way better than this, and we need to show it.’’</p><p>Counsell has shuffled the lineup, most notably by putting Pete Crow-Armstrong in the leadoff spot. He has benched regulars in the name of giving them a ‘‘mental reset.’’ It was Nico Hoerner’s and Seiya Suzuki’s turn Monday, although they pinch-hit in the ninth. He has played two recent call-ups from the minors, Kevin Alcantara and Pedro Ramirez. Except for an encouraging five runs crossing the plate in a loss Sunday to the Astros, nothing has stuck.</p><p>About the only thing Counsell hasn’t done is ask to borrow Mike Vasil’s magic wand from the White Sox.</p><p>How long can this go on?</p><p>Maybe, Crow-Armstrong suggested, we were all a bit misled by those big winning streaks.</p><p>‘‘I mean, it’s kind of felt like that all year, even with the 10-game winning streaks, like no one’s been hot at the same time, you know?’’ he said. ‘‘Like, we’ve relied on Nico for a good bit here. We relied on Ian [Happ] earlier in the year. [Busch] has been the one who is kind of solo-driving the bus. He changed today’s game with one swing.</p><p>‘‘We’ve got a lot of guys that are capable of doing that, but it’s kind of felt like that all year. Once every guy in this lineup is feeling like themselves, yeah, it’s a dangerous team.</p><p>‘‘We’re not used to putting up zero to five runs every game. We expect to have that game where we put up at least 10 once a week. We’re always on the verge of clicking at any moment.’’</p><p>There is truth in what Crow-Armstrong, who hit three balls faster than 100 mph Monday and came up empty, is saying. Hoerner and Happ were hot early, while he, Busch and Alex Bregman were struggling. Bregman just now is swinging his way out of a slump. Moises Ballesteros had a productive few weeks, then vanished, his great start lost in a horrific 3-for-51 slump. Suzuki was hurt early and has been up-and-down since. Happ is on a 200-plus-strikeout rate.</p><p>‘‘It’s all mental,’’ Crow-Armstrong said. ‘‘It’s always starting upstairs. A lot of the time, it doesn’t have to do with the game itself, as you saw [last week] with me. I think that’s an example of all of the outside factors that can affect somebody in the box that are just really naturally hard to battle with when you’re trying to hit 95 [mph] every at-bat.</p><p>‘‘But everybody in this clubhouse has a real strong mentality, and that’s just another reason we’re not ever far off from just being our true identity at its whole, at its best, at its fullest form.’’<br></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-1efe87f0-5888-11f1-b5a3-e11552ca5887"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 776px;"></td></tr></tbody></table>

entries.title: Dozens march in anti-war protest on Memorial Day in the Loop
entries.summary: <p>Army veteran Alejandro Villatoro thinks current service members should “question their oath, the position they’re in, and the decisions they’re making in other countries.”</p><p>The 44-year-old man was among dozens gathered Monday afternoon in front of the Vietnam War Memorial wall on the city’s Riverwalk, which bears the name of more than 3,000 city residents who perished in the war.</p><p>Villatoro joined Veterans Against War in 2007 and was deployed to Iraq in 2003 and Afghanistan in 2010 and 2011. He’s been a fixture of the annual protests at the monument since, and previously <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/article/world/us/veterans-symbolically-discard-service-medals-at-anti-nato-rally-idUSBRE84J0D5/" target="_blank" ><u>marched during the 2012 NATO summit</u></a>, in which he and others reenacted a 1971 Vietnam protest where soldiers threw away their medals. </p><p>He, along with others, threw his "War on Terrorism" medal, as well as NATO medals for participating in the invasion of Iraq and war in Afghanistan, toward the McCormick Place convention center fence where the summit was held.</p><p>Now, he sees a mirror of his experiences after U.S. military involvement in Venezuela, Iran and Cuba, among other places. The U.S. has <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/raul-castro-indictment-cuba-1996-shootdown-explained-fd519b43eb34c386c80ebb9b95d20197" target="_blank" >indicted </a>former Cuban President Raúl Castro<a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/raul-castro-indictment-cuba-1996-shootdown-explained-fd519b43eb34c386c80ebb9b95d20197" target="_blank" > on murder charges</a> and a U.S. blockade of fuel and other goods has caused widespread blackouts and food shortages in Cuba as war continues on the other side of the globe in Iran.</p><p>“These are billionaire wars,” Villatoro said. “It’s heartbreaking, it’s stressful. It fills me with anxiety. … One day this violence will reach home.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Ex-Cubs skipper David Ross isn't getting calls to manage again, which he reconciles as part of the business
entries.summary: <p>There are times, David Ross said, he still slips back into “Negative Town’’ when he thinks about the November day in 2023 when Jed Hoyer, the Cubs’ president of baseball operations, showed up at the door of his Tallahassee, Florida, home and blindsided him, informing him that he had been fired as manager of the Cubs and that Craig Counsell would be taking his place.</p><p>“When you first get let go,” Ross said, “it’s such a weird feeling. That first year, you’re kind of rooting for Nico [Hoerner] and [Ian] Happ and Dansby [Swanson] and all the guys that were there and played their butts off for you. But then there’s also like, I was hoping they didn’t win …</p><p>“So there’s a lot of thoughts. Sometimes, I go to ‘Negative Town.’ But I try not to. I think for the most part, I’m a pretty positive person, and I don’t like carrying stuff like that with me. That stuff’s poison for me.”</p><p>Ross was in town last weekend to shoot an episode of “The Lovable Reunion,” the podcast he co-hosts with Anthony Rizzo to coincide with the 10th anniversary of the 2016 Cubs championship team. The podcast is produced by The Volume, a sports podcast network founded by Colin Cowherd, the sports media personality and host of “The Herd with Colin Cowherd.”</p><p>“It’s been fun to do,” Ross said. “I love that people are enjoying it. It’s literally like what we would do even if we weren’t broadcasting it to the world. It’s kind of cool to put it out there.”</p><p>Ross and Rizzo were planning to interview former teammate Jason Heyward, who lives in Chicago. Ross has been back to town rarely since his firing. He came back for a Post Malone and Jelly Roll concert — he has a friend in Jelly Roll’s band — was there in January for the Cubs Convention and a couple of times for the podcast. He said hello in passing to Hoyer at the convention and recalls one brief conversation on the phone with Hoyer the first year after his firing. “He asked me about something,” Ross said. “I forget what it was.</p><p>“But I like Jed. Jed’s fine.”</p><p>He has talked on several occasions with Cubs chairman Tom Ricketts. “We just interviewed Tom for the podcast,” he said. “I saw Tom right after it happened, at Happ’s wedding, right after I got let go. We had a good conversation.</p><p>“I’ve talked to Tom more than probably anybody else. I’ll keep our conversations private.”</p><p>His first call after being fired, he told Fox’s Ken Rosenthal last year, was to Counsell, in which he congratulated him. The conversation lasted less than a minute.</p><p>For the most part, he said, he has moved on. He was on Mark DeRosa’s coaching staff for Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. He’s doing the podcast. He was hired as a studio and game analyst by ESPN — he was in Kansas City on Monday for the Royals’ Memorial Day game against the Yankees.</p><p>He divorced since his firing but sees his three children regularly. His oldest daughter, Landri, is playing Division I volleyball at the University of North Alabama. His son, Cole, will be entering his senior year of high school in the fall, plays football and intends to attend culinary school.</p><p>“I don’t know where that came from,’’ Ross said. “His mother doesn’t cook, and neither do I.”</p><p>He laughed when someone suggested maybe that’s why Cole chose culinary school — it was his only way to be sure of getting a good meal.</p><p>“He cooks on the weekends and works for a catering company and enjoys that,” he said.</p><p>The youngest Ross child is daughter Harper, who is 10.</p><p>Ross said the only time he has been back at Wrigley Field was during the Cubs Convention (“We were just mainly in the locker room”) but plans to be there for the 10th anniversary on-field celebration of the 2016 team on July 18.</p><p>“No doubt about that whatsoever,” he said. “I can’t wait to walk out on that field and be in front of the fans again. We’re here celebrating the guys that did one of the most historic things in all of sports.”</p><p>Ross admitted he initially felt some hesitation before going to the convention.</p><p>“And I did it all,” he said. “You know why? Because my brothers were doing it, and I wanted to be a part of them.</p><p>“This city is great to me, the fans. It’ll be fun to be back in Wrigley and see a packed house and be on that field. I definitely miss that.”</p><p>Ross wants to manage again. No team to date has called, even though there have been close to a dozen jobs open in the last two seasons. He has been asked about his interest in a coaching position or a staff job but to date hasn’t found what he called the right fit.</p><p>“It’s not like I sit by my phone and wait on somebody to call me,” he said. “It doesn’t really bother me. It’s like being a free agent, right? The main thing is, like, who’s reaching out to you, and who’s got interest. I think there were eight or nine [managing] jobs open this offseason, and nobody called me. That’s all the information I need to know.”</p><p>He has reconciled his firing — and the Cubs’ preference for Counsell, whom they signed to a five-year, $40 million deal — as being part of the business. He referenced this season’s firings of Alex Cora by the Red Sox and Rob Thomson by the Phillies.</p><p>“Look at what happened — two really good managers,” he said. “I’m not putting myself in their category … but I think it’s just part of the business. So I try to look at it as the blessing of going into managing a big market with no coaching experience and kind of learning on the fly in this environment. It’s part of the business. This organization has been such a big part of my life. I got to go out so well on top when I was playing, so it was bound for the baseball gods to get me back at the back end of managing.”</p><p>When Ross arrived in town Friday afternoon, he turned on the TV and watched the end of the Cubs’ sixth straight loss. He mentioned the injuries to the pitching staff, the ongoing slump at the plate, but said this, too, will pass. This team is built to go deep into October. And he’ll be rooting for it to do so.</p><p>“It’s fun to watch the Cubs,’’ he said. “I root for Justin Steele, all those guys. Part of me thinks it would be really cool to have another group of guys, 10 years later, to celebrate a championship with.’’</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Man sought in LaBagh Woods sexual assault
entries.summary: <p>Police are searching for a man who allegedly sexually assaulted a woman Saturday afternoon in LaBagh Woods on the far Northwest Side.</p><p>The incident happened about 12:30 p.m. Saturday in a heavily wooded area off-trail on the eastern side of the preserve, about 500 feet from the parking lot, according to Forest Preserves of Cook County Police.</p><p>The victim, a 29-year-old woman, was taken to Swedish Hospital and has since been released, police said.</p><p>The man suspected of the assault was described by police as a white male, about 6-feet tall with a long, brown and blond beard reaching to his chest. He was wearing a dark shirt, black beanie hat, dark sunglasses and a zip-up black jacket with a red stripe on the shoulder, police said.</p><p>Forest Preserves Police, Chicago police and the Cook County sheriff’s office have been canvassing the area since the incident and have placed heightened attention on LaBagh Woods, including increased patrols of the preserve, police said.</p><p>Anyone with information about the assault is asked to call 911.</p>

entries.title: Chicago homenajeó a los corridos con Los Tucanes de Tijuana y Fuerza Regida en el día 2 del Festival Sueños
entries.summary: <p>Quizás el único artista que logró que casi todos los asistentes en Grant Park bailaran en cojunto, Los Tucanes de Tijuana trajeron su canción clásica “La Chona” a la quinta edición del Festival Sueños de Chicago el domingo por la tarde.</p><p>Actuando en el escenario principal para una “presentación especial”, los veteranos del género norteño atrajeron a una multitud verdaderamente multigeneracional en el segundo día del evento del fin de semana del Día de los Caídos.</p><p>La alineación del domingo en Sueños fue un homenaje a la música regional mexicana, con la gran mayoría de los artistas del programa identificándose como mexicanos o mexicoamericanos. Para los residentes locales, la importancia de la selección de los artistas no pasó desapercibida, después de que Chicago y los suburbios fueron objetivo de la campaña de deportación Operativo Midway Blitz de la administración de Trump el año pasado. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/05/25/latinos-de-chicago-hacen-acto-de-presencia-y-se-lucen-en-primer-festival-suenos-desde-el-operativo-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >Los latinos llegaron al festival durante el fin de semana “hacer acto de presencia y lucirse”</a>, representando con orgullo sus culturas.</p><p>El espectro de la música de banda y norteño ha estado encabezando las listas de Billboard, Spotify, Apple y Amazon Music durante varios años consecutivos, como se mostró en <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/05/27/peso-pluma-regresa-a-suenos-con-su-primo-tito-double-p" target="_blank" >la popular actuación de Peso Pluma del año pasado</a> en Sueños. Sin embargo, la administración de Trump ha implementado cambios que endurecen las restricciones en el proceso de visas, con artistas con sede en México a quienes se les ha negado o han tenido dificultades para presentarse en los Estados Unidos.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Luego hizo una aparición como invitado con Fuerza Regida, donde cantaron “Qué onda.” Chino fue visto la noche anterior en la Taquería Atotonilco en el barrio de La Villita.</p><p>Mientras que Los Tucanes de Tijuana interpretaron los corridos clásicos que muchos inmigrantes crecieron escuchando —con temas de la vida ranchera, migración, trabajo y familia—, Fuerza Regida encarnó la letra moderna y el gusto musical de los hijos bilingües de inmigrantes que, como adultos, llevan la música mexicana a un público global.<br></p>

entries.title: Jordan Wicks will start Tuesday in place where he made stellar MLB debut
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH — It was here, in postcard-perfect PNC Park, with the dramatic backdrop of the Pirates-yellow Roberto Clemente bridge spanning the muddy Allegheny River to the city skyline on the other side, that Cubs left-hander <b>Jordan Wicks</b> made his major-league debut in 2023. A forever memory, but not the one you might have imagined.</p><p>His wife of less than a year, <b>Megan</b>, was here. Family and friends, 20 or 30 people in all, had parachuted in for the occasion.</p><p>‘‘Me and my wife talk about it all the time,’’ Wicks said Monday, the day before he is scheduled to make his first start of 2026 for the Cubs in place of injured <b>Edward Cabrera</b>. ‘‘Such a cool park to debut in, such a nice stadium, such a nice field.</p><p>‘‘I know the place was packed that night. I remember that because I gave up a homer to the first batter of the game. It got loud in a hurry.’’</p><p>This was unraveling quickly. <b>Ke’Bryan Hayes</b> hit Wicks’ second pitch of the night down the left-field line for a home run. <b>Bryan Reynolds</b> lined a single up the middle. <b>Andrew McCutchen</b> walked on five pitches.</p><p>Then came what the mike men on Marquee would call the ‘‘greatest mound visit ever.’’ That’s what Wicks remembers, at least.</p><p>‘‘<b>Tommy Hottovy</b> reminds me of it very frequently,’’ he said.</p><p>Hottovy, the Cubs’ pitching coach, made his way deliberately to the mound. You almost could feel Wicks’ heartbeat escalating with every step. Hottovy said his piece. Wicks nodded.</p><p><b>Connor Joe</b> struck out swinging. <b>Endy Rodriguez</b> looked at a third strike. <b>Joshua Palacios</b> went down swinging. Wicks struck out the first two batters of the second inning, too.</p><p>From the time Hottovy made his stroll to the mound to when Wicks came out of the game after five innings, he retired all 15 Pirates batters he faced, striking out nine. He left the game with a 2-1 lead and wound up as the winning pitcher in the Cubs’ 10-6 victory. He was the winning pitcher in his next two starts, too, becoming the first Cubs pitcher since 1901 with victories in his first three starts.</p><p>‘‘Wise, wise words from Tommy out there,’’ Wicks said.</p><p>Hottovy said he and Wicks kidded each other about it Monday. But his counsel, he insisted, didn’t rise to the level of a baseball Solomon.</p><p>‘‘Literally, all I did was remind him that he’s good, [that] you don’t have to change anything,’’ Hottovy said. ‘‘I told him: ‘McCutchen is a smart hitter. He walked on a really good changeup. You keep doing the same thing, the rest of the lineup, they want to swing.’ And he punched out the side, throwing a bunch of changeups. It was just about reminding him, ‘Your stuff’s going to play.’ ’’</p><p>Wicks was 2-4 with a 4.58 ERA in 10 starts in 2024, missing six weeks with a strained left forearm and 10 weeks with a strained right oblique. He made only eight appearances, all in relief, last season and was shut down in spring training with irritation in the radial nerve in his left forearm.</p><p>He was cleared to pitch April 18 for Triple-A Iowa and went no more than four innings in any of his first five starts. But he went six and five innings in his last two before being called up.</p><h3>Hoerner, Suzuki don’t start</h3><p>Continuing his recent practice of sitting down slumping regulars, manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> didn’t start second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> and right fielder <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> on Monday against the Pirates. Both, however, pinch-hit in the ninth inning of the Cubs’ 2-1 loss, with Hoerner grounding out and Suzuki striking out.</p><p>Hoerner, who hit four homers, drove in 22 runs and had a .908 OPS in his first 24 games, hasn’t homered in his last 29 games and is batting .198 with nine RBI and a .543 OPS during that stretch.</p><p>Suzuki hasn’t homered in 14 games since May 8 and is batting .151 with one extra-base hit (a double), two RBI and a .381 OPS in that time.</p>
